title: Jansen Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Jansen wells have a 70 ft median depth, but records range to 1,000 ft. See yields, water levels, permit history and drilling costs.
h1: What Jansen, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Jansen means understanding more than the presence of a well permit. Local records show a wide spread in depth, production and construction history across the plains around Jansen, Starkville, Trinidad and Cokedale. The typical well is relatively shallow, but the deepest recorded well reaches 1,000 feet.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records within 5 miles of Jansen. The records are useful for setting expectations, but only 32 wells report a pump yield and 30 report a static water level. Treat the local statistics as a starting point for due diligence, not a guarantee for a specific lot.

sections.heading: Jansen well depth depends on the local sediments and bedrock
sections.html:
Jansen wells have a median reported depth of 70 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 205 feet, so a driller bidding a new well here may be looking at a shallow alluvial or plains-sediment hole, but should not assume every site will be that simple. The 90th-percentile depth is 388 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,000 feet.

About 58% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 24% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 15% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 3% are deeper than 600 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That geology can make nearby well results uneven, especially where a site depends on fractures rather than a consistent shallow water-bearing layer.

sections.heading: What a Jansen well may produce
sections.html:
The reported median yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.5 and 7.6 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household uses, but it is not the same as unlimited water. Only 32 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the sample is limited.

Production is strongest in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute category, which contains 56% of reported yields. Another 28% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, 9% exceed 15 gallons per minute, and 6% are under 1 gallon per minute. A buyer should ask for the actual well test, recovery information and storage capacity. A low-yield well may still work with adequate tank storage, while a strong reported yield does not guarantee the same result on the next parcel.

sections.heading: Jansen water levels and what the records can tell you
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 35 feet, with the middle half from 22 to 37 feet below ground. That suggests many measured wells encounter water fairly close to the surface, even though total drilled depth varies considerably. Static level is not the same as pumping level, and it can change with season, nearby pumping and the time allowed for a well to recover.

Only 30 wells report a static water level, so this dataset is too small to establish a dependable long-term trend for Jansen. The permit counts also do not measure groundwater decline. Have the seller provide a current water-level measurement and pumping test where available. If you are planning a new well, a local driller can compare nearby completions in Jansen, Starkville, Trinidad and Cokedale without treating one neighboring well as proof of your site’s result.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Jansen, and when
sections.html:
The permit history shows activity across several generations. Records include 6 permits from the 1950s, 4 from the 1960s, 8 from the 1970s, 11 from the 1980s, 103 from the 1990s, 61 from the 2000s, 83 from the 2010s and 26 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025. That history shows a substantial concentration of development after the 1980s, not a uniform pace through time.

The most active named driller records are Boday Well Drilling with Alex Boday listed on 56 wells and Kathleen Boday listed on 42. Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 55 records. These names can help when comparing construction styles or asking for local references, but a permit history is not a recommendation. Verify licensing, insurance, scope and the proposed casing and grout details before hiring.

sections.heading: Jansen well drilling cost at the typical depth
sections.html:
For Jansen’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,400 to $3,800. That is only the hole. It does not cover the complete water system needed to use the well.

The modeled finished-well cost is about $8,400 to $15,800, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical. A contractor’s bid can move outside that range if the well needs more depth, different casing or grout, difficult access, additional trenching or treatment equipment. Ask for a written breakdown separating drilling, casing, grout, development, pump installation, electrical and testing. The deepest recorded wells show why a shallow-depth allowance should not be treated as a guaranteed final price.

sections.heading: Jansen risks: water quality, low yield and site layout
sections.html:
Permit records identify 117 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Jansen, along with 224 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped area. Those figures do not tell you whether a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test existing well water and review the property’s location and past use.

Low yield and dry-hole risk remain separate from water quality. A well can be deep and still produce poorly, or a shallow well can need careful protection from surface entry. Check casing, grout, wellhead drainage and the distance from septic components. Colorado DWR permit terms matter too: domestic or household wells have defined uses, and an exempt well is subject to the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Confirm water rights and any augmentation requirement before planning irrigation, multiple homes or other expanded use.

sections.heading: Before buying or building on a Jansen lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then pull every nearby permit rather than relying on a countywide average. Focus on reported depth, aquifer name, yield, static level, construction notes and the well’s permitted use. The local records show 358 wells, but only 176 are recorded as constructed, 236 report total depth, 32 report pump yield and 30 report static water level. Missing data is common.

For an existing home, require a current flow or pressure check, laboratory water testing and a review of the pump, tank, electrical service and septic system. For vacant land, confirm access for a rig, likely well location, septic setbacks, building envelope and the DWR permit path before closing. A driller should inspect the site and discuss a contingency if the first hole is dry or produces less than the home requires. Do not price the entire project from drilling footage alone.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Jansen, Colorado?
faq.a: Jansen wells have a median reported depth of 70 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 205 feet, but the range is wide: the 90th-percentile depth is 388 feet and the deepest recorded well is 1,000 feet. About 58% are under 100 feet, so shallow wells are common but not guaranteed.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Jansen?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,400 to $3,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $8,400 to $15,800. Greater depth or difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Jansen?
faq.a: Reported Jansen wells have a median yield of 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.5 and 7.6 gallons per minute. About 56% of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 6% are under 1 gallon per minute. Only 32 wells report yield, so test the specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Jansen?
faq.a: You cannot determine safety from a permit map alone. There are 117 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 224 historic mine features within about 10 miles, although there are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well through a qualified laboratory and review casing, grout, septic placement and property history.

faq.q: Do Jansen wells have a falling water table?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a reliable falling-water-table trend. Only 30 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 35 feet and a middle half from 22 to 37 feet. Those measurements are useful for comparison, but they are too limited to prove long-term change. Request current measurements and pumping information.
